meta.title: Guided tours
meta.status: Draft, for a biology teacher to review.
notes: A tour is a list of steps in order. Each step has a title, text to show, an optional question for the class, and a target saying what the app should open.

target.view is one of: "map" (the genome map); "chromosome" (one whole chromosome, with chromosome); "gene" (a chromosome zoomed to one gene with its card open, with chromosome and gene); "region" (a gene region, with region); "variant" (a variant's letters and card in its region, with region, variant and showVariantVersion).
A "region" target shows the whole region unless it also has gene and jump. jump is "codingStart" and means the same as the "Go to start of coding" button for that gene.
showVariantVersion says whether the "Show variant version" switch should be on when the step opens.

Every number in the text was filled in from genome-overview.json, genes.json, gene-regions.json and variants.json when this file was built, so it matches what the app shows from those files. Rebuild this file if any of them changes.
Tours describe well-established science in plain words. They are not medical advice.

sources.name: HELIX data files
sources.provider: Built from GRCh38, GENCODE release 46, HGNC and gnomAD v4
sources.usedFor: Every number and every target in the tours
sources.terms: See the sources listed in each of those files.

tours.title: From a chromosome to a protein
tours.summary: Zoom from the whole genome down to the letters of one gene, and read the start of the protein it codes for.

steps.title: The whole genome
steps.text: These are the 24 different human chromosomes, drawn to scale. Together they hold 3,088,269,832 letters of DNA and 19,398 protein-coding genes. The bars beside each chromosome show where the genes are.
steps.question: Which chromosomes look crowded with genes for their size, and which look nearly empty?

steps.title: Chromosome 11
steps.text: Chromosome 11 has 135,086,622 letters and 1,280 protein-coding genes. The genes are not spread evenly. Some stretches are packed with them and others have very few.

steps.title: One gene: HBB
steps.text: This is HBB, the gene for beta-globin, part of the haemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood. It is 1,608 letters long. On a chromosome of 135,086,622 letters, that is a very small target.
steps.question: If chromosome 11 were a road 135 kilometres long, about how long would HBB be?

steps.title: Exons and introns
steps.text: Up close, HBB is in pieces. The boxes are its 3 exons, and the thin lines between them are introns, which are cut out before the protein is made. Its neighbour HBD is built the same way. Both genes are read from right to left.

steps.title: Reading the letters
steps.text: Here are the DNA letters where the coding part of HBB begins. Read in threes in the gene's direction, each group of three letters stands for one amino acid. The first is always methionine. The whole protein is 147 amino acids long.
steps.question: Only 444 of the gene's 1,608 letters are coding. What fraction is that, and what is the rest for?

tours.title: One letter: the sickle cell change
tours.summary: See how changing a single DNA letter changes one amino acid in haemoglobin, and think about why that version is still found today.

steps.title: The gene
steps.text: HBB carries the instructions for beta-globin. Two markers sit above the gene. Each one marks a place where some people's DNA differs from the reference by one letter.

steps.title: One letter
steps.text: This is the sickle cell change. At position 5,227,001 the reference has T and this version has A. Nothing else in the gene is different.

steps.title: One amino acid
steps.text: With the variant version showing, amino acid 7 is valine where the reference has glutamic acid. That one swap changes how haemoglobin molecules stick together when oxygen is low.
steps.question: The protein has 147 amino acids. Why can changing just one of them matter so much?

steps.title: The letter next door
steps.text: A different change, one letter along, alters the same amino acid in another way. Here amino acid 7 becomes lysine. The result is a version of haemoglobin called haemoglobin C.

steps.title: How common is it?
steps.text: Among the people in gnomAD, about 1 in 380 gene copies carries the sickle cell change. It is much more common in places where malaria has been common, because people with one copy are partly protected against malaria.
steps.question: People with two copies have sickle cell disease. How can a version that causes disease stay common in some parts of the world?

tours.title: Three kinds of change
tours.summary: Compare a change that alters no protein, a change that cuts a protein short, and a change that removes one amino acid.

steps.title: A change outside the code
steps.text: This change is not in a coding part of any gene. It lies in an intron of MCM6, 13,907 letters before the coding part of LCT begins, and no protein changes. It sits in a switch that controls LCT, and people with this version usually keep making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, as adults.
steps.question: How can a change alter what a body does without altering any protein?

steps.title: An early stop
steps.text: In ACTN3, one changed letter turns the code for arginine into a stop signal. The protein ends after 576 of its 901 amino acids. Among the people in gnomAD, 43.9% of gene copies carry this version, and people with two copies are healthy.
steps.question: What does it tell you about a protein if many healthy people make none of it?

steps.title: Three letters missing
steps.text: In CFTR, three letters are missing in this version. The reading in threes carries on unbroken, but one amino acid, phenylalanine at position 508, is left out of a protein that is 1,480 amino acids long. People with two copies of this version have cystic fibrosis.
steps.question: Why does losing three letters do less damage to the reading than losing one or two would?

steps.title: Compare the three
steps.text: You have seen a change that alters no protein, a change that removes more than a third of one, and a change that removes a single amino acid. The size of a change in the DNA does not tell you the size of its effect on a person.
steps.question: Which of the three changes alters its protein most? Which matters most for health? Are those the same?
